conflicts/northern-crusades/name: The Northern (Baltic) Crusades and the Teutonic Order
conflicts/northern-crusades/religionRole: Papal bulls from 1147 onward granted crusade indulgences for war against the pagan Wends, Livs, Estonians, Prussians and Lithuanians, and the military orders existed to wage holy war; conversion of pagans was the constant stated goal, at times explicitly by force. Yet conquest, the founding of bishoprics and towns, German and Scandinavian settlement, tribute, the fur and grain trade and the territorial state of the Teutonic Order were equally real motives. Eric Christiansen and William Urban stress this mixture; Polish and Lithuanian historiography long saw the Order as a vehicle of German expansion, and the crusades after Lithuania’s baptism in 1387 were openly contested as lacking any religious justification.

conflicts/northern-crusades/summary: From 1147 the papacy extended crusading to the pagan peoples of the Baltic. Saxons and Danes attacked the Wends; German bishops, merchants and the Sword Brothers conquered Livonia; Danes took Estonia and Swedes Finland; and from 1230 the Teutonic Order conquered Prussia and fought Lithuania for two centuries. Converts were often baptised at sword-point, and the Order built a powerful state. Lithuania’s baptism in 1387 removed the rationale, and the Polish–Lithuanian victory at Grunwald in 1410 broke the Order’s power.
conflicts/northern-crusades/story:
During the preaching of the Second Crusade in 1147, Saxon princes asked to fight their pagan Slav neighbours, the Wends, instead of going to the East. Bernard of Clairvaux urged them to fight until either the pagans’ religion or the nation itself was destroyed, and Pope Eugenius III’s bull Divina dispensatione granted the crusade indulgence. The Wendish Crusade besieged Dobin and Demmin and marched to Stettin, which was already Christian; it achieved little, but it set the precedent. Over the next decades Henry the Lion and the Danish kings conquered the Wendish lands, and in 1168 Valdemar I of Denmark and Bishop Absalon took Arkona on Rügen and destroyed the great idol of Svantevit.

Further east, German merchants and the missionary Meinhard reached the Livs on the Daugava in the 1180s. After resistance, popes granted crusade privileges for Livonia, and Bishop Albert of Buxhoeveden founded Riga in 1201 and the Order of the Sword Brothers in 1202. The Chronicle of Henry of Livonia describes a cycle of raids, hostage-taking and baptisms of whole districts after defeat. Danes under Valdemar II conquered northern Estonia from 1219, when tradition says the Dannebrog flag fell from heaven at Lyndanisse (Tallinn). Swedish expeditions brought Finland under Swedish and Catholic rule in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. In 1236 the Sword Brothers were destroyed by Samogitians and Semigallians at Saule, and their remnant was merged into the Teutonic Order.

The Teutonic Order, founded at Acre in the 1190s, was invited by Duke Konrad of Masovia to fight the pagan Prussians, and Emperor Frederick II’s Golden Bull of Rimini (1226) and later papal grants gave it rights to the conquered land. From 1230 the knights advanced along the Vistula, building castles at Thorn, Kulm, Marienwerder and Elbing, with crusaders arriving each season from Germany and beyond. The Prussians rose in 1242 and in the Great Prussian Uprising of 1260–1274 under leaders such as Herkus Monte; the Order suppressed them with great severity, and many Prussians were killed, deported or reduced to dependence, their language dying out by the seventeenth century. In 1242 the Livonian branch’s attack on Orthodox Novgorod was defeated by Alexander Nevsky on the ice of Lake Peipus, a battle later magnified by Russian national memory.

Lithuania remained the great pagan power. Its ruler Mindaugas was baptised in 1251 and crowned king in 1253 but broke with Christianity around 1261. Under Gediminas and his sons Lithuania expanded into Orthodox Rus’ while resisting the Order. Through the fourteenth century the Order staged ‘Reisen’, seasonal raids into Samogitia and Lithuania joined by knights from across Europe, including Henry Bolingbroke, the future Henry IV of England, in 1390–1392; Chaucer’s Knight had ‘reysed in Lettow’. These raids burned villages and carried off captives, while Lithuanian raids devastated Prussia and Livonia in turn.

In 1385 the Union of Krewo united Lithuania with Poland: Grand Duke Jogaila was baptised in 1386, married Queen Jadwiga and became King Władysław II, and in 1387 Lithuania accepted Catholic Christianity, with Samogitia following in 1413–1417. The Order nevertheless continued to wage war, claiming the conversion was false. On 15 July 1410 the Polish–Lithuanian army defeated the Order at Grunwald (Tannenberg); Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen and much of the Order’s leadership were killed. Marienburg survived the following siege and the First Peace of Thorn (1411) cost the Order little land, but its power and prestige were broken.

At the Council of Constance (1414–1418) the Polish canonist Paulus Vladimiri argued that pagans possessed legitimate rights to their lands and could not be attacked merely for unbelief, while a Dominican defender of the Order, John Falkenberg, called for the killing of the Poles and their king and was condemned. The Thirteen Years’ War ended in the Second Peace of Thorn (1466), which made the Order a Polish vassal, and in 1525 its grand master Albrecht of Brandenburg-Ansbach turned Prussia into a Lutheran duchy. The Livonian branch survived until 1561.
conflicts/northern-crusades/nameOfGod: Crusaders received the cross and indulgences comparable to those for Jerusalem, and from the 1190s Livonia was presented as the ‘land of Mary’ (Terra Mariana), whose conquest was service to the Virgin. Bernard of Clairvaux’s call to fight ‘until either the rite itself or the nation be destroyed’ became notorious. Henry of Livonia’s chronicle describes the war as the spread of the faith and the baptism of pagans after their defeat. The Teutonic Knights, a religious order bound by vows, held the castle of Marienburg as the ‘castle of Mary’ and treated war against pagans as a form of devotion.
conflicts/northern-crusades/religiousCau: Papal extension of the crusade indulgence to wars against pagans on the frontiers of Christendom, beginning with Eugenius III’s bull Divina dispensatione in 1147.
Missionary failure among the Livs and Prussians, which led bishops to call for armed protection and forced conversion.
The vocation of the military orders, the Sword Brothers and the Teutonic Knights, which needed a field of holy war, especially after the loss of the Holy Land.
Marian devotion, which cast Livonia and Prussia as lands consecrated to the Virgin.
Hostility to Orthodox ‘schismatics’ in Novgorod and Pskov, which at times extended the crusade against fellow Christians.
conflicts/northern-crusades/otherCauses/: German, Danish and Swedish territorial expansion and the desire for land, tribute and lordship.
Commercial interests of Lübeck and the merchants of the later Hanseatic League in the Baltic trade routes, furs, wax and grain.
The Teutonic Order’s ambition to build a sovereign state, and its rivalry with Poland over Pomerania and Danzig.
Settlement of German peasants and townspeople in Prussia and the Baltic, encouraged by lords and the Order.
Chivalric prestige: the Reisen offered knights from France, England and the Empire a place to earn honour after crusading in the East ended.
conflicts/northern-crusades/triggers/0: Saxon reluctance to go East during the Second Crusade, answered by Bernard of Clairvaux and Eugenius III’s authorisation of the Wendish Crusade in 1147.
conflicts/northern-crusades/triggers/1: Pagan attacks on the mission at Üxküll in Livonia in the 1190s and the death of Bishop Berthold in 1198.
conflicts/northern-crusades/triggers/2: Konrad of Masovia’s invitation to the Teutonic Order in the 1220s to defend his lands against Prussian raids.

conflicts/northern-crusades/timeline/3/t: Valdemar II of Denmark conquers northern Estonia at Lyndanisse (Tallinn).
conflicts/northern-crusades/timeline/4/t: Golden Bull of Rimini grants the Teutonic Order rights to Prussia; conquest begins in 1230.
conflicts/northern-crusades/timeline/5/t: Sword Brothers destroyed at Saule; merged into the Teutonic Order in 1237.
conflicts/northern-crusades/timeline/6/t: Alexander Nevsky defeats the Livonian knights on Lake Peipus.
conflicts/northern-crusades/timeline/7/t: Treaty of Christburg, mediated by a papal legate, guarantees rights to baptised Prussians.

conflicts/northern-crusades/casualties/n: No meaningful total can be given for wars spread over more than two and a half centuries and largely recorded by the victors. Chronicles describe the burning of villages, killing of men and enslavement of women and children on all sides. Grunwald involved perhaps 15,000–30,000 men per side in modern estimates and cost the Order several thousand dead, but even these figures are disputed. The demographic collapse of the Old Prussians is attested by the later extinction of their language rather than by counts.
conflicts/northern-crusades/effects/0: Livonia, Estonia, Prussia and Finland were brought into Latin Christendom under German, Danish and Swedish lordship, with lasting social divisions between German elites and native peasants.
conflicts/northern-crusades/effects/1: The Teutonic Order built one of the most efficient states of late medieval Europe, later the core of the Duchy and Kingdom of Prussia.
conflicts/northern-crusades/effects/2: The Old Prussian people and language were largely destroyed or assimilated.
conflicts/northern-crusades/effects/3: Lithuania chose baptism from Poland rather than conquest by the Order, creating the Polish–Lithuanian union that dominated eastern Europe for centuries.
conflicts/northern-crusades/effects/4: Conflict between the Latin crusaders and Orthodox Novgorod and Pskov fixed a lasting frontier between Catholic and Orthodox Christianity.
conflicts/northern-crusades/effectsOnChu: New Latin bishoprics were founded at Riga, Dorpat, Ösel, Kulm, Pomesania, Ermland, Samland and elsewhere, many controlled by or allied to the Order.
Christianisation was often superficial at first; pagan practices survived in rural Livonia and Lithuania for centuries.
Crusading against fellow Christians after 1387 provoked debate at Constance about the rights of pagans and the limits of holy war.
In 1525 Prussia became the first Lutheran territorial state, and Livonia turned Lutheran in the following decades.
conflicts/northern-crusades/legacy: The Northern Crusades created the religious map of the Baltic and left contested memories: the Teutonic Knight became a symbol of German aggression in Polish, Lithuanian and Russian nationalism, notably in Sienkiewicz’s novel The Knights of the Cross and Eisenstein’s film Alexander Nevsky, while German nationalists, and later the Nazis, appropriated the Order as a symbol of a ‘Drang nach Osten’. Modern scholarship treats them as a distinctive branch of crusading in which mission, conquest and colonisation were inseparable.
conflicts/northern-crusades/dissenters/0: At the Council of Constance he argued that infidels have lawful dominion over their lands and may not be warred upon or forcibly converted simply because they are not Christians.
conflicts/northern-crusades/dissenters/1: In his Opus maius (1267) the Franciscan wrote that pagans of the Baltic were willing to accept the faith peacefully but that the brothers of the Teutonic Order wanted to subjugate and enslave them.
conflicts/northern-crusades/dissenters/2: Papal legate Jacob of Liège (later Pope Urban IV)

Mediated the Treaty of Christburg (1249), which guaranteed baptised Prussians personal freedom, property and legal rights against the Order, though the guarantees were later disregarded after the uprisings.
conflicts/northern-crusades/dissenters/3: Archbishops of Riga and Livonian bishops

Repeatedly complained to the papacy in the fourteenth century that the Order hindered missions and mistreated converts; in 1312 the papal legate Francesco de Moliano excommunicated the Order in Livonia after hearing such charges.
conflicts/northern-crusades/campaigns/0/: Saxon princes, Danish forces and bishops, including Albert the Bear
One army gathered at Magdeburg and marched via Havelberg to besiege Demmin and then Stettin, where it found crosses on the walls of an already Christian city; another, with the Danes, besieged Dobin.
conflicts/northern-crusades/campaigns/1/: The Teutonic Order’s conquest of Prussia
The Teutonic Knights with seasonal crusaders
The knights advanced down the Vistula and along the Vistula Lagoon, building castle-towns as they went, and founded Königsberg in 1255 after a crusade led by King Ottokar II of Bohemia.
conflicts/northern-crusades/campaigns/2/: The Polish–Lithuanian army under Władysław II Jagiełło and Vytautas

The allied armies crossed the Vistula on a pontoon bridge at Czerwińsk, outflanked the Order’s position on the Drwęca, won the battle of Grunwald on 15 July and besieged Marienburg until September without taking it.
